hints: Look carefully at compound Z and list every functional group it contains, not just the carbonyls.
Recall that NaBH4 is a selective reducing agent that reduces aldehydes and ketones to alcohols but leaves C=C bonds untouched.
With excess reagent, both carbonyl groups will be fully reduced, so track how each C=O changes to C-OH while the alkene stays the same.
walkthrough:
**Identify the functional groups in Z**

Look at the structure from left to right. You have an alkene, a ketone in the middle, and an aldehyde on the right.

Structure: $CH_2=CH-CH(CH_3)-C(=O)-CH_2-CHO$

**Recall what NaBH4 does and does not do**

NaBH4 is a mild reducing agent. It reduces aldehydes to primary alcohols and ketones to secondary alcohols.

$$R-CHO \rightarrow R-CH_2OH$$
$$R_2C=O \rightarrow R_2CH-OH$$
It does NOT reduce C=C alkenes. That needs $H_2$ with Ni/Pt catalyst.

**Apply excess to both carbonyls**

Because excess is used, both reductions go to completion. The aldehyde $CHO$ becomes $CH_2OH$ and the ketone $C=O$ becomes $CH-OH$.

Product skeleton: $CH_2=CH-CH(CH_3)-CH(OH)-CH_2-CH_2OH$

**Match to the correct structure**

This is a diol that still contains the original $C=C$ double bond on the left. That matches exactly one of the given structures.

options.A: Correct. Both the aldehyde is reduced to a primary alcohol ($CH_2OH$) and the ketone is reduced to a secondary alcohol ($CH-OH$), while the alkene $CH_2=CH-$ is unchanged. This is exactly what excess NaBH4 does.
options.B: Incorrect. This shows the correct diol but the C=C bond has also been reduced to an alkane ($CH_3CH_2-$). NaBH4 never reduces alkenes, a common confusion with catalytic hydrogenation or with stronger LiAlH4 ideas.
options.C: Incorrect. This shows the alkene reduced but both carbonyls unchanged. It gets the selectivity completely backwards, NaBH4 reduces C=O, not C=C.
options.D: Incorrect. This shows only the aldehyde reduced to $CH_2OH$ while the ketone is left as $C=O$. With excess NaBH4 both aldehydes and ketones are reduced, so this would only fit a limited or controlled amount, not excess.
